By analyzing the behavior of the Bardeen potential and the power spectrum, it was found that a specific time period during inflation when the power spectrum becomes negatively skewed is linked to the development of large negative values in the Bardeen potential. Additionally, a specific amplitude of the power spectrum was identified and related to the magnitude of the Bardeen potential, which raises implications for the cosmological perturbation theory, particularly its behavior during the inflationary period.

Research into the structure of ordered trees has been limited by a lack of random generation methods. To address this, we developed an algorithm to randomly generate standard ordered trees based on a specific set of parameters. By analyzing these trees, we found the average number of deepest nodes to be approximately 0.5, which is not significantly different from the average number of marked nodes in the same set of trees. This finding challenges a previous hypothesis regarding the structure of ordered trees.

To enhance the accuracy of optical character recognition in vote counting, a effective spell correction method is crucial.  Although Levenstein distance-based techniques yield respectable results, improving upon this is still a research area worth exploring. One such advancement involves utilizing binary CMAC hash codes to achieve better performance.  In this paper, we introduce a more efficient Levenstein distance calculation technique utilizing a binary Maximal-And Minimal Covering placement algorithm.  This algorithm generates optimal solutions across various code lengths, producing the least complex sets required to encompass all possible Levenstein distances, thereby enabling fast spell correction.

In the training of traditional linear models, applying Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) typically yields stable and accurate results, even with infinite-dimensional data features. However, the emergence of artificial neural networks (NNs) has shown them to be a powerful tool for complex function approximation, yet their sensitivity to dimensional explosion remains an unresolved issue. Currently, many models, including those with time-dependent variables, often result in data beyond the finite-dimensional realm. Therefore, developing methods to handle high-dimensional data with linear components is a pressing concern. By drawing parallels between SGD and NNs, leveraging techniques such as multi-task learning and neighborhood methods, we propose novel approaches to tackle infinite-dimensional data features. Our methods can be applied to over-parameterized linear models, and our theoretical analysis confirms their convergence and accuracy. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical effectiveness of these techniques through concrete applications. Our code is openly accessible on https://github.com/hucheng2004/InfinityData.

Recently, a novel scheme using bidirectional attention has been shown to achieve high quality speech synthesis.  Although this method produces natural-sounding speech, the architectural restriction of separate encoders for speech and noise prevents it from effectively handling complex real-world noise scenarios. To overcome this limitation, a new multi-input attention model is proposed in this paper. The proposed model combines speech and noise representations using a single bidirectional encoder, with two separate decoders for synthesis, using attention-based summation. This architecture is particularly useful for handling real-world noise scenarios involving complex backgrounds. The proposed system is evaluated on the CMU-ARC dataset, and the results show significant improvements in objective quality and naturalness compared to existing attention-based methods, with a mean opinion score (MOS) scores of 3.76 and 3.68 for clean and noisy conditions, respectively.

The fundamental responsibility of a pressure sensor system in aircraft navigation and control systems lies in providing reliable and accurate pressure data to calculate altitude and ascent/descent rates. This paper will investigate the possibilities of weakening a differential pressure sensor (DPS) system in an aircraft navigation and control system using a non-cooperative jamming attack. First, we will examine the consequences of a single pressure sensor (SPS) system compromise, including the manipulation of ascent/descent rate calculations and resulting position discrepancies. Secondly, we will explore the implications of compromising a DPS system across different attack scenarios, including those involving various attack intensities and locations. Our findings indicate that a DPS system compromise can lead to significant position errors, particularly when the attack occurs during the aircraft's ascent phase. Importantly, we will also highlight the differences between our DPS and SPS system attack scenarios, demonstrating that the latter produces more pronounced altitude errors due to increased sensor noise, whereas the former is more susceptible to attack-induced oscillations. To mitigate these attacks, we propose a technique involving the implementation of an attack detector and a resilience strategy that integrates multiple sensor readings to enhance system reliability.

As the transition to variable renewable energies progresses, managing energy storage in a way that reflects risks associated with intermittent generation and changing electricity demands becomes increasingly important. We've developed mathematical models that account for risk-averse storage management, considering different levels of risk averseness and time-varying electricity demands. Our analysis of these models reveals storage management strategies that minimize the probability of exceeding a certain capacity under future uncertainties, and we find that a optimal storage policy can be obtained through a transformation of the model that depends on the level of risk averseness. We demonstrate that being risk-averse during specific periods can lead to storage management that differs significantly from the results obtained through traditional methods, and that this difference can have a substantial impact on the overall costs of the energy system. Finally, we find that only the most extreme levels of risk averseness lead to storage being charged during peak hours, and that moderate risk averseness tends to prioritize charging during peak hours over discharging, with further research needed to fully capture this effect.

Researchers from several institutions, including Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden, and Lund University, Lund, Sweden, have conducted an experimental and theoretical analysis of the coherent electron motion within core-excited states in nitrogen gas, using x-ray pulses from the free-electron laser in Hamburg, Germany. By adjusting the energy of these x-ray pulses, they were able to intentionally match certain energy levels, causing the electrons to go into a state of high momentum. As expected, a sudden change in the crystal structure around these excited atoms was observed. Furthermore, the researchers were able to modify this effect by changing the time between excitation and return to the ground state, ultimately leading to the destruction of the excited state and the emission of x-ray photons. The ability to control the motion of these electrons opens up possibilities for the development of new optical technologies that could potentially operate at a much faster pace than current technologies.

Our research involves incorporating an Earth-like atmospheric circulation pattern into a Martian general circulation model. The model successfully replicates the baroclinic storms observed on Mars using a simplified atmospheric configuration, which can be used to investigate atmospheric processes. The simulation shows that the featureless Martian terrain doesn't hinder the development of persistent storms, and these storms exhibit the same characteristics as those found on Earth, with similar patterns forming in the mid-latitudes. The Martian atmosphere exhibits the expected circulation patterns when subjected to Earth-like conditions, with the formation of horse latitudes, wind reversals, and storm systems. These storms move westward and release heat, causing local temperature increases, ultimately shaping the Martian landscape into its current form.

Current active learning algorithms are task-specific and tend to excel on smaller datasets like LVPC, yet they fall short when dealing with larger datasets like ImageNet. This research investigates the possibility of deploying the same active learning method across multiple tasks within a dataset. Our study employs three prominent deep learning algorithms and evaluates their performance on two visual classification datasets. The results show that traditional methods such as dual clustering and recursive clustering can be applied to large-scale datasets like ImageNet with minimal modifications. However, when attempting to leverage multiple tasks within the dataset, their effectiveness significantly declines. Conversely, newer algorithms like BALD consistently deliver superior performance, even when confronted with multiple tasks within large-scale datasets like ImageNet.

Researchers have been seeking to define a comprehensive concept of algebraic multiplicity that encompasses various existing measures. This study introduces a novel, generalized definition tied to the Schur operator and demonstrates its distinctness from existing measures. Additionally, a specific formula is presented to calculate the proposed measure for non-degenerate matrices.

We examine a variable-input, fixed-basis measurement attack on two-mode squeezing-aided optical phase sensing. Our analysis reveals that two-mode squeezing's enhancing effect on sensitivity can be circumvented, and that users should limit the amount of two-mode squeezing to match the baseline system's gain, which originally arises from converting single-photon correlations into usable gain. Additionally, we show that two-mode squeezing's utility in optical phase sensing can be reaped when users have control over input variables, as this allows them to employ a variable-basis measurement attack, thus rendering the sensing system's improvement permanent.

Using a combination of theoretical modeling and experimental measurement in a planar terahertz time-domain spectroscopy system, we analyzed the operation of two-qubit gates based on neutral donor atoms in silicon. We examined the impact of positioning and optimizing the donor atoms, as well as the influence of temperature, electric field, and interface charge on the success of these gates. Our results indicate that certain arrangements of donor atoms can minimize the detrimental effects of these factors, ultimately achieving high fidelity (>99.9%) for two-qubit operations despite their influence. Furthermore, we found that certain gate placements can facilitate the use of two-qubit gates with independent qubit control, eliminating the need for a global operational sequence. This research provides valuable insights into optimizing two-qubit operations utilizing neutral donor atoms in silicon, a crucial step for developing large-scale quantum computing systems.

In macroscopic samples, we've observed a persistent oscillation in magnetic resistance just above the zero Landau level, which can be explained by a combination of scattering events within the quantum well and its contact to skimming electrons.

This research proposes an adaptive cooperative nonorthogonal multiple access (AC-NOMA) protocol that learns optimal strategy parameters to minimize outage probability, and we theoretically prove its performance is superior to existing cooperative Noma protocols using fixed parameters in terms of outage probability. We also derive an optimal parameter value for the proposed AC-NOMA protocol and provide numerical simulations to verify our theoretical findings.

This research focuses on addressing power allocation and scheduling concerns in mobile networks that can change how cells operate. To model this process, we use an optimization technique and examine its performance with different methods, also evaluating how a key system efficiency is affected when different cells communicate at the same time. To speed up computations, we investigate alternative approaches and find one that causes the system to perform nearly as well. This solution is then tested under realistic conditions and compared with existing strategies.

We have investigated the behavior of vortices in a two-dimensional strong-flavor QCD using lattice QCD, with a focus on how their motion is affected by the formation of chiral condensates. By analyzing the motion of isolated vortices and those accompanied by soliton-like objects called instanton molecules, we found that their motion is governed by different activation energies. While soliton-like vortices require significant energy to move, vortices may be moved by lower energy levels, often associated with the formation of meson-like objects. These findings suggest that vortices can exist independently, driven by these lower energy levels. Our study also reveals that the motion of isolated vortices is impacted by the formation of meson pairs, resulting in a activation energy that is equivalent to that of soliton-like vortices. Notably, we found that the motion of both types of vortices is aligned with that of superconductors, with the motion of vortices occurring in the opposite direction to that of the external pressure.

Researchers examined the effects of a external magnetic field on the normalized cumulants of energy in lattice systems near their critical temperatures, using the Ising model as a basis. The study explored a range of external fields and variously shaped lattices in both parallel and perpendicular orientations, with results indicating a notable connection between the normalized cumulants and external field at the critical temperature. In particular, the behavior was found to be consistent with skewness in a broad range of field strengths, and calculations were also performed using a Monte Carlo simulation to verify theoretical predictions.

This study introduces three novel families of 4-tensors that are closely tied to matrix product operators in 2-dimensional topological order, extending upon a similar 2-dimensional tensor previously studied. By incorporating a unitary matrix, these 4-tensors can be transformed to represent the equivalence classes desired for gauge symmetry, ultimately facilitating explicit construction of the corresponding parent Hamiltonians using a parent Hamiltonian construction framework. As a significant advancement, this work enables the precise, analytically derived parent Hamiltonians for various paradigms of topological order, including string-nested, topological order, and certain gapped domain wall interpretations, by applying the parent Hamiltonian construction framework. Moreover, this research provides the distinct parent Hamiltonians for different gauge equivalence classes, which can be distinguished based on their periodic boundary properties. Furthermore, this work offers a novel perspective on the 4-tensor structure, representing the physical essence of the corresponding matrix product operators, which can be utilized to extract valuable information about the physical properties, such as the fusion category associated with the 2-dimensional topological order.

We introduce a new methodology for testing the capabilities of artificial intelligence systems that solve physical problems and their potential applications in solving other complex problems. This methodology evaluates whether machines learning Hamiltonians and laws of physics can generalize to solve other physical tasks, even those from unrelated domains. We developed a Hamiltonian Neural Network and an LSTM-based meta-learner to learn the dynamics of various systems, including a harmonic oscillator, double spring system,, and falling cat, and demonstrated these models' ability to predict physical behaviors and inferred their Hamiltonians. When tasked with predicting the motion of unfamiliar systems with similar dynamics or spring physics applied to unfamiliar geometries, these models exhibited the ability to generalize. A Hamiltonian Neural Network outperformed an LSTM-based meta-learner on multiple tests, and both models successfully applied their knowledge to solve other physical problems in related domains, even those with significant spatial transformations. However, the LSTM-based meta-learner failed to generalize to categories of physical behaviors it had not encountered during training, demonstrating a limitation of both approaches.

In the context of incremental and dynamic data, a method has been proposed to create a multi-agent system. This system considers the trustworthiness of machines learning models to optimize decision-making processes and ensure the stability of the learning process. Each agent in the system represents an instance of a regularized deep learning model, with a unique parameterization that ensures optimal performance on a specific subset of data. The system works in a decentralized manner, with agents sharing their model parameters and corresponding data subsets. This allows for the creation of a cohesive model that achieves high accuracy and low error rates on unseen data, thus minimizing the risk of model instability. This approach outperforms existing incremental machine learning methods, with improved accuracy and trust scores, while maintaining the simplicity of previous models. The system's effectiveness is demonstrated through applications to image classification using the CIFAR-100 and Fashion dataset, and natural language processing using the 20Newsgroups dataset.

Airports need to effectively identify prohibited items to prevent terrorism and ensure public safety. However, the quality of current security scans is often compromised, making the task more difficult. Existing research has addressed the challenge of interpreting medical images, but there's a significant gap in research regarding the interpretation of scanning devices used in security checks. To bridge this gap, we've created a large dataset of x-ray images featuring prohibited items, containing over 10,000 images representing 10 different categories of forbidden goods. The dataset is uniquely diverse, as the images vary significantly in quality and background, obtained directly from x-ray scanning devices employed by major airlines. Our experimental findings demonstrate the importance of selecting appropriate evaluation metrics for x-ray image classification tasks, as they have a significant impact on the accuracy of the models. Interestingly, our research indicates that using a simple residual network outperforms more complex models like InceptionV3 and SeResNeXt. Additionally, we've discovered that leveraging the dataset's diverse images offers no significant advantage when compared to training on a smaller subset of more representative images.

Recent research reveals that the modified Jones polynomial, introduced by some authors as $J_n^T$, significantly simplifies the structure of its coefficients for various types of links. Specifically, its properties hold true for twisted knots and braids, suggesting a potential connection to the braid axis property. This study further explores $J_n^T$ by examining its polynomial extensions, establishing that its coefficients exhibit the same structure for links in the realm of the Collins-Gutierrez-Rosso braid invariant. In this context, $J_n^T$ can be viewed as a link polynomial invariant that simplifies the structure of its coefficients for twisted knots and braids.

Data augmentation has been widely adopted as a successful means of enhancing dataset resilience and reinforcing deep learning models for natural language processing tasks. We undertook a comprehensive exploration of data augmentation methods in sentence-level text classification, investigating both widely accepted techniques and relatively unexplored methods. We conducted exhaustive experiments across three popular models and five standard datasets, demonstrating the consistent benefits of data augmentation in sentence-level text classification. Moreover, we established guidelines for optimizing data augmentation settings based on both automatic and human evaluations. Our findings revealed that a carefully optimized, lightweight method termed Levenshtein Mutation outperformed other data augmentation strategies. We further introduced an open-source framework called JDataAug, providing simple and efficient data augmentation tools that excel over existing complex implementations.

This paper explores the connection between the Hankel path and the Wright beta function through a complex representation of the Gamma function. By analyzing the derived relationship, we establish the associated integral representation of the Hankel transform of mild type for functions defined on the real line. Additionally, we demonstrate the connection between the Hankel path and the Gamma function by establishing a related result involving the Gamma function within the context of the Hankel transform.

Recent measurements of top quark production cross-sections by the ATLAS and CMS collaborations at the LHC have yielded results for top quark isolated production, top quark pair production, and top quark pair production with additional jets. These data, covering various luminosities and energy configurations, are compared to perturbative quantum chromodynamics (QCD) predictions, with calculations accounting for experimental detection inefficiencies and incorporating threshold-resonance perturbation theory for low-energy data. These predictions are based on next-to-leading order QCD theory and supersimplify the process of evaluating theoretical predictions, also facilitating the derivation of scale-uncertainty estimates in line with the recommendations of the PDF4LHC group.

The current version of the Hadoop MapReduce SQL system, DRadoop, relies on a physical plan to layout data placement and execution order. Nonetheless, this plan is crafted without knowledge of actual data within tables, which poses a significant challenge during query processing. Furthermore, the absence of data information leads to inaccurate enhancements, often resulting in suboptimal performance, in addition to causing difficulties in determining certain rows and columns during execution. In our research, we present an innovative way to refine the accuracy of plan executions based solely on data that is actually present, without needing access to the entire database. In doing so, we introduce an entirely new approach to update query plans, one that takes into consideration the presence of data, even in the absence of comprehensive database knowledge. In our experiments and real-world applications, this method has demonstrated a notable capacity to improve plan accuracy. In particular, our results show that this method can effectively enhance execution accuracy even without access to the entire database, which is the focus of our research. In fact, in our experiments and real-world applications, this method has proven so effective that we can achieve superior execution accuracy with access to as little as 10% of the entire database, a finding that is both intriguing and validating of our research. In our research, we have also introduced various strategies to refine plans in relation to data availability, which we believe will be beneficial in enabling the exploration of more complex optimization techniques. In our research, we have chosen to build upon the physical optimization

This paper explores the challenge of estimating privacy losses in complex graph-structured data sets, particularly those with interconnected points. Existing research on differentially private learning has overlooked the implicit information exchange between connected data points. To address this gap, we establish a mathematical framework to quantify the enhanced privacy risk triggered by interconnected data points and establish a lower bound for privacy loss computation. Additionally, this paper introduces actionable insights for optimizing privacy losses in specific types of graph structures, specifically random geometric graphs and ring structures. Our methods are versatile and applicable to various privacy mechanisms, including the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms. To facilitate practical application, we develop a computational tool that can compute lower bounds and provide relative error estimates for various graph settings. This research lays the groundwork for exploring new graph structures and advancing our mathematical understanding of privacy loss in complex data sets.

The planned Euclid mission by the European Space Agency (ESA) will gather significant amounts of data on the cosmos, particularly in the fields of astronomical research. To ensure the scientific value of this data, it's essential to simulate the observations Euclid will make and then use those simulations in the analysis of the actual data collected. This process involves using the characteristics of Euclid's spacecraft and instruments to create realistic simulations of the data that would be collected during the mission. This paper describes the software needed to perform this simulation and data collection, including the configuration and testing of the systems. It also explains the approaches that will be used to analyze the data collected from Euclid, including various techniques for selecting samples and analyzing data. The software described in this paper is currently the standard approach for analyzing Euclid data and will likely be replaced in the future as the mission prepares for launch in late 2022.

To create highly reliable automated lane-keeping systems, it's essential to simulate complex road networks that can challenge these systems. Unfortunately, developing such systems is a time-consuming and expensive process due to technical limitations of current testing methods. To accelerate the development process and make testing more efficient, this study proposes a novel approach to generating realistic and difficult road scenarios. These scenarios are designed to trigger specific failures in automated lane-keeping systems, allowing developers to identify and fix underlying issues. By developing a set of synthetic evaluation tools, this study demonstrates the benefits of this approach in detecting and rectifying faults in automated lane-keeping systems.

The appeal of music lies not only in its melodic quality but also in the memories it evokes, which are often tied to specific times and places. Amidst the vastness of the internet, choosing music manually is a time-consuming task. As a result, automated music recommendation systems are in high demand. These systems extract valuable insights from audio content, allowing for the creation of personalized playlists tailored to individual tastes. This special issue of the IEEE/ACM AIPR journal highlights the latest advancements in music information retrieval, covering various techniques that enhance recommendation systems' effectiveness.

We present a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme for evaluating quantum hydrodynamic equations, which minimizes artificial oscillations in simulations. This method effectively maintains accurate results for non-equilibrium correlation functions despite the reduction in oscillatory behavior. To illustrate its effectiveness, we apply the linearized scheme to a simple quantum lattice gas model and observe a significant improvement in simulations of late-time correlations, especially in scenarios where the equilibrium state is reached quickly.

Recently, deep convolutional networks have achieved significant success in generating action proposals from video. Introducing the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), an end-to-end video proposal network that refines action proposal production. Can be found on arXiv.

This study explains the emergence of a specific frequency range, known as the palm tree mode range, where edge localized modes (ELMs) and magnetic islands previously dominated the frequency spectrum. The PTMs frequency range now occupies the space once held by these modes/islands as they have shifted to higher frequencies, now often seen in the late ELM phase or within magnetic island structures. Two distinct scenarios, one featuring a highly turbulent ELM and the other with a magnetic island, are analyzed using the power spectral density (PSD) of edge resolution interferometry and edge magneto-optical scissors. The development of PTMs is linked to the intersection of rational surfaces with the edge magnetic field and is influenced by the edge magnetic connectivity and current. This relationship is explored further in a simplified edge current model. The model indicates that changes in the edge current profile, caused by magnetic connectivity defects, result in the activation or deactivation of PTMs. This understanding has implications for improving edge resolution in plasma studies.

Mobile robots that navigate through their surroundings and avoid collisions can use potential fields as a navigation tool. By assigning negative values to areas they should avoid and positive values to areas they want to reach, these robots can find a path to their destinations while bypassing obstacles. A limitation of this method is that it can become stuck in an infinite loop if it detects an infinite potential field. To mitigate this, a technique was developed that defines the potential field based on fluid dynamics. However, this approach only considered planar movements and didn't account for rotations, and a similar model also existed. For a robot with the ability to rotate and move in three-dimensional space, a new potential field model was created that takes into consideration these movements and prevents the robot from getting trapped in infinite loops. A algorithm was then developed to determine the potential field for a specific scenario and was applied to a three-dimensional navigation test.

We establish a frequency large deviation principle for a renewal process in its tail exponent, which applies to both infinite and finite horizon time periods. This renewal process analysis is then utilized to investigate the specific case of stationary processes, such as those generated by a sequence of independently and identically distributed letters, where we demonstrate the existence of a quenched large deviation principle for the distribution of their empirical measures. This is particularly evident for ergodic processes with periodic properties, for which the renewal process analogy helps us determine the likelihood of observing particular sequences of letters within a given time frame.

In scenarios where the line-of-sight link between a radar and its target is weak or obstructed, an Intelligent Reflecting Surface can enhance performance by providing an alternative, active reflection for detection and tracking purposes. This paper chemically complements our initial study on optimizing an IRS's reflection pattern to improve radar reception, by also considering the situation where the line-of-sight link is not completely cut off and has some underlying strength. We model this interaction as a multi-antenna system with a line-of-sight link, an IRS with multiple passive units, and a target. Our objective is to minimize the radar's transmission power while maintaining a desired signal-to-noise ratio in the presence of this line-of-sight link and the IRS. We derive an optimized reflection pattern for the IRS and provide a hybrid optimization method that can be applied when the line-of-sight link strength is known, unknown, or falls into any interval of possible strengths. Our results show that the optimal reflection pattern occurs when the strongest line-of-sight link is either the weakest link overall or significantly stronger than the second strongest. Furthermore, if the line-of-sight link is the weakest link overall, the optimal reflection pattern can be achieved through a simple, low-complexity method.

Modern fuzzing tools, capable of generating persistent and complex inputs,
complicates the evaluation of testing tools. While recent mutation analysis
techniques enhance fuzzer assessment, they remain underrepresented in current
research. Furthermore, existing studies primarily focus on individual tools,
leaving the comparison of fuzzers as an open issue. To address these challenges,
we propose a comprehensive mutation analysis framework for validator-based
fuzzers. Our approach incorporates a persistent check to assess the robustness
of generated inputs and a complex input measurement to evaluate functional
preservation. By applying this framework to four renowned fuzzers, including
LLFMAP, FFUF, ZAP, and Hof, we investigate the effectiveness of our method and
the similarities and differences it reveals in fuzzer behavior. Our results
show that even subtle variations in fuzzer code can lead to significant
robustness differences in persistent inputs, while all fuzzers excel in
withstanding validation checks but exhibit functional degradation under complex
inputs. Nonetheless, our findings underscore the importance of validating
fuzzer assessments through independent means.

This research investigates a key challenge in continual learning: incorporating new classes to a existing class hierarchy. We test the ability of neural networks to recognize new classes using a diverse dataset of image categories, and assess their performance using a simple learning method that has already been established as a relevant benchmark. Our results show that deep learning models can effectively learn to recognize new classes even after a long period of continuous learning, and that their ability to do so does not depend on the order in which the classes are introduced. Additionally, we find that using pretrained models significantly enhances the ability to learn new classes and that the Nearest Mean Classifier, a basic method using pretrained features and weights, is comparable to state-of-the-art continual learning algorithms and outperforms them in some cases. Finally, we observe a phenomenon we refer to as "expansion bias" where the error rate for newly introduced classes consistently decreases as more classes are added, and propose a straightforward technique to mitigate this bias.

If a map to a 2-dimensional complex, $X$, from a 4-dimensional complex, $Y$, shares the same homotopy class as a map that factors through a 2-dimensional complex, $X_0$, then we demonstrate that there exists a $Z$, which factors through $X_0$, such that $Y$ is homotopic to $Z$. This condition holds under the assumption that the homotopy class of maps from $Y$ to $X$ is non-trivial. Additionally, if the connected component of the identity in the group of maps from $Y$ to $X$ is trivial, then we can establish that there exists a $Z$, which factors through $Z$, and $Z$ is homotopic to $Z'.

The paper investigates the long-term behavior of solutions to a particular partial differential equation at a stable equilibrium point, where the equilibrium point has a specific stability property. This property is maintained for a specific, relatively short period of time. It is demonstrated that solutions with certain initial conditions will asymptotically approach a specific, lower equilibrium point, where this asymptotic behavior is supported by numerical data and various theoretical arguments. The paper also presents a theoretical framework for studying equations of the type $u_t=u_{xx}+\lambda f(u)$, where this framework implies that solutions will approach a stable equilibrium point under specific conditions. This framework is applied to a specific equation to analyze the asymptotic behavior of solutions, where this results in the identification of a stable equilibrium point and a specific frequency of oscillation. This frequency of oscillation is influenced by the strength of the nonlinear term and the stability of the equilibrium point, where this is demonstrated through numerical data and theoretical arguments.

The 64Ni nucleus, with its significant neutron subshell gap at N=40, provides an ideal framework to study the monopole interaction and the evolution of excitation energies. Investigating the monopole character of 2+ and 4+ states in 64Ni and its relatives, our analysis highlights how the monopole interaction shapes the excitation spectrum across different neutron configurations. A notable phenomenon observed in 64Ni is the increased separation energy between its 2+ and 4+ states, which can be attributed to the robust N=40 subshell gap. This effect, however, diminishes with increasing neutron number, and in 66Ni, the monopole interaction's influence on the excitation spectrum is more apparent, resulting in a more standardized separation pattern. Our study emphasizes the importance of considering the neutron configuration's impact on the monopole interaction and the excitation spectrum's formation.

We analyze generalizations of Lipschitz games known as structured Lipschitz games, where each player has an associated Lipschitz constant. These generalized games fall under the category of quasi-concave games that retain the simplicity of lipschitzness. We establish a connection between structured lipschitz games and the linear programming formulation of standard lipschitz games, revealing that structured games can be viewed as a projection of standard games onto specific compensation matrices defined by player-specific lipschitz constants. Additionally, we investigate efficient algorithms for computing structured lipschitz payoffs through linear programming and least-squares methods, along with an innovative strategy that combines these approaches. Our proposed method involves transforming the structured game into an equivalent standard lipshitz game, solving the resulting linear programming problem, and deriving the structured lipshitz payoff as a projection of the standard lipshitz payoff.

Our investigation into the reliability of machine learning models suggests that average performance estimates are inherently unstable and vary significantly depending on the specific split of data into training and testing groups, particularly in scenarios with limited data. This finding leads us to examine a common validation technique, k-fold cross validation, and its effectiveness in achieving robust performance estimates. The evaluation of different k values, including one proposed by Hernandez-Garcia and Gil, reveals that increasing k with a fixed number of iterations yields more stable performance estimates, essentially mimicking the results of using a much larger dataset. In effect, using k-fold cross validation is equivalent to using a dataset with k times the number of observations for the majority of k values. Consequently, we propose Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD) as a more suitable metric to assess the stability of performance estimates, yielding a clear picture of the stability landscape for each k value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using k-fold CV with a value close to the number of observations (k ≈ N) significantly improves the stability of performance estimates, surpassing the stability achieved with larger datasets, thereby allowing machine learning models to effectively utilize all available data.

Recent advancements in neural networks have been driven by Self-Training techniques, which have made transferring knowledge to smaller networks possible. This has generated significant interest in Teacher-Student architectures, where a complex teacher network successfully trains a lighter student model. The goal of this study is to enhance the ability of these architectures to learn from mistakes. We delve into the mechanism of how Teacher-Student architectures facilitate the performance of lightweight student networks compared to deep teacher networks and explore potential areas for improvement. Additionally, we examine and contribute to the development of several key factors that influence the performance of these architectures across various categories, including semantically-related categories, domains with limited data and overlapping categories. Our findings suggest that Teacher-Student architectures excel in domains with significant differences, but may not be as effective in scenarios with more similar domains. We explore several techniques to improve these architectures by utilizing additional data, adapting to new domains and introducing a new method that focuses on correcting specific mistakes. Our proposed approach leads to improved performance and enhances the ability of these architectures to learn from errors.

Bucket Elimination is an efficient algorithm for performing inference and optimization within graphical models, particularly those represented as CSPs or with binary variables and certain types of constraints. By reorganizing variables into structured groups that facilitate rapid elimination, Bucket Elimination can outperform other methods, such as TRWBT and BT. However, determining optimal bucket structures can be non-deterministic, making the algorithm suitable for parallel processing. In our research, we introduce a novel heuristic approach, called BE*, which involves iterative bucket refinements and elimination updates, leveraging both local tractability and issue-driven strategies, and is compatible with various optimization objectives. We demonstrate BE*'s effectiveness through comparative experiments against BE and other state-of-the-art algorithms, and provide the BE* algorithm in an easily usable Python class for public access.

We've derived an modified absorption lineshape model that accounts for photon recoil in a high-saturation light absorption scenario. Our approach utilizes a Gaussian distribution for the change in wavelength due to photon recoil. We find that photon recoil results in the shifting of absorption features in certain situations and can also lead to the creation of new absorption resonances alongside existing ones. However, these new resonances would likely fall within the wings of the primary absorption resonance and so might be difficult to identify with current experimental techniques. Furthermore, we observe that the spread of the lineshape is influenced by the change in wavelength due to photon recoil, especially in situations with high-saturation levels.

We establish a common framework for both isotropic jamming and shear jamming models, whether they involve frictionless or frictional conditions, by utilizing a scalar variable to characterize the point of jamming. Through this approach, we gain a deeper understanding of the relationships between different jamming exponents, and our findings indicate that frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming exhibit distinct critical behaviors, separated in time and space. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the shear jamming model can be further divided into two categories based on its response to strain and stress, and that these categories also display different exponents, which reflect the complexities inherent in the shear jamming model near its point of instability.

The paper investigates the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the centralizer Z(n)(sl2) through its connection to the Hilbert-Poincaré series of the braid group Bn, which is achieved by using the Coxeter graph invariant framework introduced by J. Levine. A key aspect of this investigation is expressing the Hilbert-Poincaré series of Z(n)(sl2) as a sum of coefficients multiplied by the Hilbert-Poincaré series of irreducible Bn representations. Additionally, the paper provides a formula for calculating the coefficients in front of the irreducible Bn representation Hilbert-Poincaré series in Z(n)(sl2)'s Hilbert-Poincaré series. A key technical aspect of this approach involves applying a variant of the Lascoux-Leclay algorithm to achieve this goal.

A key characteristic of magnetic systems with spatially dependent interactions, gratifying an internal symmetry, is the absence of spontaneous symmetry breaking when interactions like Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya are absent. Our research reveals that these systems exhibit unique topological properties when interactions like Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya are present, which can be controlled through an external magnetic field. This control is achieved by adjusting the strength of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions relative to that of dipolar interactions, which are modulated as a result of the applied field. Consequently, this modulation triggers a transition from non-trivial to trivial phases of matter and vice versa, which can also be influenced by the direction of the applied field. Ultimately, this finding suggests that these systems may be suitable for the realization of topological phases of matter that are difficult to obtain in other contexts.

We examine the scenario of Weakly Interacting Massive Particles (WIMPs) annihilating in a uniform density field and calculate the number of final-state photons produced through the conversion of plasmon WIMPs. Considering a velocity distribution that accurately reflects the average WIMP velocity, we find that the predicted photon spectrum is significantly lower than estimated by assuming a one-dimensional velocity distribution. Furthermore, by comparing our one-dimensional velocity distribution with numerical simulations of WIMP motions, we identify an underlying structure that could be utilized to derive a more general velocity distribution function. Additionally, we explore the possibility of observing the WIMP photon spectrum with upcoming experiments such as the Simple Astronomical Magnetic Spectrometer (SAMS).

This study undertakes a thorough examination of the current understanding of algorithmic biases in Web search engines, particularly focusing on their impact on users who rely on simplified search interfaces and require more accurate, detailed information. Although previous research has identified the presence of algorithmic biases, little attention has been dedicated to exploring their effects on users who lack technical search skills. To bridge this knowledge gap, our work investigates the prevalence of algorithmic biases in search engines, its underlying causes, and its overall significance within the public sector contexts. Multiple sources were consulted to develop a comprehensive theoretical foundation, which in turn guided the design of a quantitative survey aimed at gathering information from a representative sample of public sector professionals. The collected data was subsequently analyzed to reveal the prevalence of algorithmic biases, their causes, and their effects on the mentioned context. Furthermore, the research identified various mitigation strategies, which can be leveraged to address the associated risks. Additionally, our work highlighted the importance of raising awareness among public sector professionals regarding the presence of algorithmic biases in search engines and the potential consequences of their unaddressed use.

Research into next-generation particle colliders, which could reach TeV scales in energy, is currently ongoing. These colliders have the potential to explore fundamental questions about matter and the universe by producing highly energetic particle interactions and subsequent detection of resulting subatomic particles, such as muons, electrons, photons, and others. We examine potential production processes of particles at these facilities, which could involve combinations of these subatomic particles, including processes like pair production, forced creation, and processes related to Higgs boson interactions. The capabilities of these colliders when operating at TeV scales would allow for in-depth study of various phenomena, including the creation of dark matter, the production of extra dimensions, and the observation of new heavy particles. Additionally, in some cases, the new particles generated could decay directly to known particles, making their detection possible with existing experiments, such as those operated by Fermilab. We also consider how a muon collider might be beneficial for certain research areas and propose possible layouts for such a collider when operating at energies between 1-10 TeV, which could potentially enhance the accuracy of associated experiments by 10-100 times.

This paper introduces a new non-uniform sampling technique known as ranked compressed approximate sparse point response sampling (rCASPR) that leverages compressed sensing principles to collect fewer, more representative point-spread function samples. By using rCASPR, we demonstrate the ability to achieve higher image contrast and point-spread functions with fewer point responses. Comparative evaluations with traditional linear sampling reveal significant improvements in point-spread function and image contrast. Additionally, the rCASPR algorithm proves adaptable across various imaging systems, easily transferring its benefits to these systems.

This research paper proposes a novel method for creating optimal feedback control policies in complex robotic systems subject to safety constraints. This approach is based on an interesting connection between two distinct concepts: Higher Order Control Barrier Functions and Interval Calculus-based Feedback Controllers. To build on this foundation, we demonstrate that any ICCBF can be represented as a specific type of HOCBF, and vice versa. This equivalence in structure forms the basis for our proposal to utilize HOCBFs as a more versatile framework that includes ICCBFs. To effectively solve the optimal control problem, we leverage a key property of HOCBFs and employ a feasible direction search algorithm within the safety constraints. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we apply it to a case study involving a nonholonomic mobile robot navigating a straight path.

Continuous domain theory combines continuous lattices with continuous functions through CPO-domains and Scott-continuous functions. However, this framework overlooks certain essential topological properties captured by CF-approximation spaces. These spaces embody the continuous structure of CPOs via Scott-continuous functions and Hausdorff proximities. Certain subsets in a CF-space are 'determined' or CF-closed, which is a key concept for union operations, fixed points, and continuous lattices. This study specifically focuses on fixed points of union operations within the context of CF-closed subsets and investigates whether the structure of such subsets can be continuous. In doing so, it establishes that the associated function space corresponds to a continuous domain and examines various properties of this domain. This research also expands on existing results concerning fixed points of union operations, which is fundamental for applying the laws of continuity in CF-spaces.

This research introduces an exact paired-permutation test implementation, along with a new Monte Carlo approximation. The exact method, based on the convergence of Friedberg series, enables highly effective sampling with essentially no computational expense. In contrast, the approximate method utilizes random number generation to achieve a significant time reduction, despite not guaranteeing precise results. Through benchmarking against real-world data, the exact algorithm demonstrates superior performance, with the friedberg-based sampler showcasing improved efficiency in comparison to the approximate method.

This paper examines the recent collapse of shipping cartels, specifically in the tanker sector, following a 2017 antitrust ruling. To understand the consequences, a theoretical model of competitive and collaborative shipping strategies is developed and numerically analyzed. According to the model, the absence of cartels leads to increased freight prices and shipping volumes for certain commodities, closely aligning with observed data from 2017 to 2021. The study also reveals that smaller shipping groups have a clearer incentive to defy cartels and benefit from the resulting price increases. Furthermore, in order to prevent former cartel members from regaining dominance, it's essential to maintain vigorous antitrust enforcement.

Loom structures were initially defined by K. Devlin and M. Goldsmith in 2009 as a special type of loom space that allows for the construction of a triangulation. Here, we demonstrate that every loom space has an associated triangulation, based on this definition. This finding elevates loom structures to a higher topological category, giving loom spaces a similar status to construction spaces. Additionally, this research provides a new characterization of loom structures through a decomposition of loom spaces into simpler components. Our approach uses the concepts of cut-loom spaces and construction prescripts.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) combine the capabilities of wide deep learning architectures and flexible modeling frameworks, consistently showing high accuracy in resolving complex graph-based tasks. However, little research has focused on exploring the potential of training GNNs, particularly in situations where training data consists of sparse graphs. Our study reveals that graph structure plays a crucial role in GNNs' predictive ability, with contributions ranging from 0.077 to 0.337 in certain tasks, surpassing the influence of node features. We propose an innovative approach called graph mean average precision (GMAP), measuring the diversity of GNNs' predictions based on the structure of their output graphs. GMAP exceeds the established metric mean average precision (MAP) in accuracy, providing a clear picture of the relationships between GNNs, PAC-Bayes bounds, and the diversity of their predictions. Finally, our findings lead to several significant conclusions, including the statement that GNNs can always achieve optimal training losses, despite experiencing a significant reduction in performance when faced with limited training data. Our results also emphasize the critical role of diversity in GNNs, stating that this factor contributes more substantially to their accuracy than node features. Finally, we predict that under certain conditions, which are theoretically provable, the performance of GNNs will continually improve with the increase of data density.

We offer a mathematical framework for analyzing the performance of dimension reduction methods, which provides robust results despite issues with data contamination. Our study demonstrates that by utilizing an adaptive input, in conjunction with suitable estimator adaptation, we can achieve the optimal rate for a specific structure - specifically for minimizing the $\ell_2^2$ risk, in a random design setting, in the context of inductive methods. Our framework is particularly effective in addressing concerns related to the collection of adaptive inputs, which may contain valuable information but is also potentially flawed. We derive explicit bounds that demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and showcase the methodology with traditional estimators, which includes an unexpected improvement in estimation accuracy.

This paper builds on our previous findings regarding compact areas with singular points in the Euclidean space of two dimensions, specifically addressing those that minimize volume within a given constraint in the presence of various geometries. We continue to employ the approach established in [6], where key properties of these compact areas were determined through surgery-style arguments. In this context, we aim to further advance the understanding of these geometries by investigating the associated singular sets and flat patterns when the associated compact areas develop symmetries. Our investigation into such cases yields several important conclusions, which provide greater insight into the geometry of these compact areas and their singular sets. Additionally, our results identify specific conditions under which the associated compact areas exhibit radial symmetry, while also demonstrating that such symmetry necessarily leads to the formation of angles less than pi in the associated singular sets. We also demonstrate that when the associated compact areas develop certain other geometries, namely those resembling the geometry of a double cone, certain rotationally symmetric configurations become volume-optimal in the presence of certain constraints, thereby addressing a key aspect of our initial problem.

A moving magnetic flux line inside a superconductor causes entropy to distribute between the vortex core and the moving charge carrier cloud, often referred to as the Clem entropy. Despite being a fundamental concept in the theory, the exact entropy within the vortex core has remained unknown until now. By utilizing a combination of experimental Gd dopant scattering and theoretical modeling, we have successfully measured the entropy in the vortex core for a range of temperatures and vortex velocities. Our findings indicate that the total entropy remains constant at any given velocity, but is divided between the vortex core and the cloud in a temperature-dependent manner, shifting towards the cloud as temperature increases. Additionally, we discovered that the cloud's entropy contribution follows the same universal function as the heat capacity of the cloud, and that the entropy within the vortex core is significantly more limited, displaying a more intricate temperature velocity dependence.

The fast growth of decentralized energy sources and flexible loads necessitates an revolutionary new way for an aggregator to communicate with a system operator. This breakthrough lies in using information-theoretic methods to maximize entropy feedback, which we apply to a scenario where the operator needs the aggregator to follow specific targets regarding peak reduction and load shape. A diverse array of loads with distinct characteristics poses a challenge, but an advanced controller can tackle this issue by continuously estimating the expected outcome based on past performance and update its strategy accordingly. By leveraging the structural properties of this complex system, we are able to create an efficient algorithm that yields near-optimal results and demonstrate its effectiveness with a simulated example utilizing real-world data.

Our research offers a predictive model that uses multiple technical indicators and historical stock prices to forecast future performance. Many investors rely on technical analysis, using indicators and looking at past trading data to inform their decisions. Our model builds upon this approach by combining 10 widely used indicators, drawing from 20 years of daily stock price data. We tested various prediction methods and selected 3 that exhibited consistency and low risk, ultimately training the model using nearly 20 years of data from the S&P/ASX 200. Our results indicate that the model can accurately predict future performance, specifically 1-day, 5-day, 20-day and 40-day returns. We found that the model performs well in forecasting the overall market trend and identified situations where it performed exceptionally well, primarily during periods of high volatility. Interestingly, our findings suggest that the model's performance improves during times of significant market upheaval. We also discovered instances where certain stocks' predictions varied significantly from the overall market trend, indicating that the model may be useful in identifying opportunities within the market.

All known binary supernovae can be attributed to one of the following four scenarios: (1) compact object mergers, (2) massive star mergers, (3) collapse of massive stars, or (4) mergers involving white dwarfs. Research suggests that the last of these options accounts for the largest share of supernovae, at approximately 50%. When white dwarfs merge, they do so at high speeds, resulting in a collision that produces sparks of electromagnetic energy and, ultimately, a bright supernova. This process is hypothesized to be responsible for the origin of SAG-NB: a rare class of supernovae characterized by mild expansion and moderate energy production. Analysis of available data on paired white dwarfs provides insights into the variety of supernovae that can arise from these collisions, which can take the form of both conventional and rare explosions. Furthermore, research indicates that many of these paired white dwarfs possess high orbital energies, which can lead to the production of soft gamma repeaters and pulsars. This understanding of paired white dwarfs' diverse roles in the cosmos raises the possibility that some of their explosions might have been misclassified as standard supernovae explosions.

This research investigates the double Higgs production mechanism within the Standard Model Effective Field Theory and its effective field theory counterpart, Higgs Effective Field Theory. We develop a relevant effective theory description for the double Higgs process and its associated decay, considering the Standard Model's primary output - the di-photon channel. We establish a correspondence between these two theories for their leading coefficients and derive relevant cross-section and rate expressions. We also introduce a distinction between physical masses and the minimum cut parameter in the effective theory, which affects the cross-section and associated decay rates. As a result, we obtain more accurate rate predictions for the double Higgs production process and its decay into a di-photon system.

We extend the 'pre-non-relativistic' approximations commonly used for gravitational waves in expanding cosmological backgrounds. This approach allows for an analytical expansion of general relativity's metrics in expanding cosmological backgrounds, making it feasible to compute the gravitational waves emitted from scalar field inflation. The method is demonstrated by first introducing the 'pre-non-relativistic' approximations, and then modifying the metrics to account for an expanding cosmological background. The consequences of this are that the background metric's time-dependent components are represented by the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker metrics, and the spatial components are expressed as an analytical expansion of the harmonic series. The conformal metric is also defined for the perturbed metrics, from which the gravitational waves can be derived. The simplicity of the 'pre-non-relativistic' approximations makes it easy to analyze the waves' amplitude and spectrum. The method is validated by calculating the perturbation metrics and the differential energy density fluctuations. The approach offers a flexible framework for incorporating additional background metrics beyond the Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker metrics. The code used for these computations is publicly accessible.

We have developed a novel numerical strategy for solving general relativity's Einstein equations in the 3+1 dimensional framework. This method involves dividing the equations into two distinct sets of differential equations, which can be solved independently to compute the gravitational variables and the congruence of geodesics. Since the spatial metrics' evolution does not depend on the second set of equations, solving the Einstein equations for the gravitational variables becomes a simpler boundary value problem. Additionally, the fact that the boundary observables are calculated from the geodesics' behavior allows for a more direct approach. By utilizing the Einstein equations' decoupled form, we can determine the observed values at the boundary without resolving the full equations, which can be useful for implementing boundary conditions. This method is particularly beneficial for simulations involving compact objects with complex structures, where numerical instability might be an issue.

Our experimental investigation examines how a cylindrical intruder moves through different types of granular materials at varying speeds, focusing on its long-range flow effects. We studied two types of monodisperse and bidisperse granular layers, observing the intruder's motion over several intruder diameters and found that it transitioned from a steady state to a time-averaged state. The drag experienced by the intruder was measured in both steady and time-averaged states, and we discovered that the average drag increased with the square of the intruder's speed, but was influenced by the driving rate in the time-averaged state. Additionally, we found that the drag experienced by the intruder varied with the square of the bed's friction coefficient in the steady state, but was linked to the bed's friction and intruder-to-grain size ratios in the time-averaged state.

Using observations from ALMA and GMRT, we studied a starbursting galaxy, TDE 01.MS.mittal.01, which exhibited massive ionized gas outflows. By analyzing the galaxy, we found that the outflows are likely fueled by the starburst and contribute significantly to the galactic disk's gas depletion. Despite boosting the galactic wind energy by 15 times, the starburst still maintains a significant gas supply, likely due to the energy increase not leading to gas heating until it reaches the wind's edge. The enhanced wind might influence future star formation in the galaxy's center, and through multiple spherical shells, the galaxy shows a symmetric ionized gas structure, likely the result of interacting major mergers.

BoAnon introduces an innovative technique to find efficient configuration settings by leveraging blockchain nodes with unique parameters and a novel anomaly-detection method. Existing methods for discovering optimal parameters require significant time, resources, and data, whereas BoAnon facilitates the process by finding acceptable settings in real-time, even with a large dataset, by implementing a check-verify process on the blockchain. Furthermore, BoAnon improves the detection of irregular transactions by implementing a dynamic approach based on Conway-Maxwell-Bloch processes and checking for anomalies in a batch-based manner. This method enhances energy efficiency and accelerates anomaly detection, enabling BoAnon to handle a high-frequency FTS and efficiently find acceptable parameter settings.

The star subtraction procedure, a method used to eliminate background from two-particle angular correlation measurements, has a significant impact on the results of transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow from p-Pb collisions. By comparing charged particles and identified particles such as pions, kaons, and protons, this study finds that once background is removed, the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow and elliptic flow follow a similar trend. Additionally, this trend holds true for p-Pb and Cu-Cu collisions. However, when background is included, the transverse momentum dependence of triangular flow differs from that of elliptic flow.

Large-scale RDF datasets, which are increasingly popular, require an efficient assessment of data quality. This task is complicated by the complexity of RDF data and the variety of quality issues it can exhibit. Existing quality assessment approaches for RDF data are limited in number and focus primarily on specific aspects of data quality, such as consistency and completeness. Furthermore, they are designed to operate on small-to-medium sized datasets. To address these challenges, we have developed an innovative quality assessment framework for large-scale RDF datasets, called DQA. This system utilizes a two-pronged strategy, involving both lightweight in-memory techniques and highly optimized disk-based methods, to evaluate the quality of entire datasets rather than individual triples. Additionally, DQA includes a high-level query language that allows users to define quality criteria with ease, and its results can be utilized to identify data entities in need of correction, generate data visualization, and inform data consumption decisions. To support our claims, we have conducted a comprehensive set of experiments, incorporating real-world datasets and benchmarking DQA against existing RDF processors.

This study examines the performance of minimum density power divergence (MDPD) estimators in comparison to maximum likelihood (ML) estimators for various dependent processes using simulation techniques. MDPD and ML estimators were computed using an iterative method, and the results were combed for the fewest standard deviations and the smallest bias among the estimators. Depending on the model, the best results were obtained with ML, MDPD with $\delta=0.5$, or MDPD with $\delta=0.7$. Notably, MDPD estimators outperformed ML estimators for processes involving dependent increments, and often provided a notable improvement in bias reduction. Conversely, in scenarios where the process' dependence has a limited impact on data, using ML estimators may be sufficient. A key consideration is that the success of these dependent processes' estimators may rely on the specific parameters used, and therefore, it would be beneficial to further mathematically define the dependent processes' estimators' standard deviations and biases.

The intricate mixing of gas in the hearts of active galaxies remains poorly understood despite significant research. The reason for this is the abundance of processes involved, including shock-ionization, which can significantly alter gas appearance and properties. To better comprehend observable characteristics of gas, like their level of ionization, temperature, and chemical composition, and how they're affected by the active galactic nucleus, you need to develop a robust model that incorporates these processes and their effects. This work presents a new model based on a network of ionizing reactions that allows it to calculate the energy deposited into gas by shock-waves and the resulting ionization patterns. Using this model, researchers can now predict how gas appears in different scenarios, such as variations in gas density and the frequency of prompt post-outburst ionization. This research is further illustrated by a numerical study of gas behavior following a significant outburst in a compact system.

The Internet of Things (IoT) is becoming a vital part of the connected world, where the convergence of physical and digital elements is driving the necessity for swift and efficient IoT applications. Although rapid development is possible with lightweight languages and tools like Rake and RakeScript, ensuring the reliability of these applications through thorough testing remains a significant challenge. To aid this process, we introduce the Frisbee framework, which empowers developers to create automated testing scenarios for IoT applications via a simple and intuitive command-line interface. By providing a comprehensive solution for testing IoT applications, Frisbee promotes a best-practice approach to coding and encourages collaboration among developers.

The search for rare occurrences of B meson decay into a muon pair has led to an investigation of two processes: B^0_s to mu+ mu- and B^0 to mu+ mu-. A new analysis by the LHCb collaboration has significantly enhanced its understanding of these events by meticulously examining all related data sets. With the full 9 fb^-1 batch of LHCb data at its disposal, including results from running at 13 TeV, the study has achieved a maximum sensitivity for B^0_s to mu+ mu- at a decay rate 5.8 x 10^-7 times standard. Additionally, this analysis has also set a minimum for B^0 to mu+ mu- at 2.6 x 10^-8 times standard, with this limit for the latter process being the most restrictive constraint to date. Both of these results have been consistently in line with the predictions of the Standard Model of particle physics.

The advancement of self-driving vehicles relies heavily on accurate traffic scene modeling.
Current approaches primarily focus on individual object recognition, leaving the scene's overall
structure and context unexplored. To address this limitation, we introduce SceneGen, a comprehensive
approach to modeling traffic scenes. Building upon a type-group hierarchy of traffic objects, we establish
a hierarchical relationship between objects, background, and scene context. Our approach incorporates
a hierarchical instance selection mechanism and a multi-stage conditional generator to model complex
traffic scenes, ensuring consistency with real-world images through a pair of discriminators. By generating
a diverse range of scenes and evaluating our method's performance on the Lyft dataset, we demonstrate
SceneGen's capability to model sophisticated traffic scenes and showcase potential uses of scene models
for self-driving vehicle training data generation. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/
autotrace/SceneGen.

Consider a Cayley tree structured graph, where the Ising model's partition function can be calculated using the group representation of a non-Abelian group, specifically the dihedral group D_n, depending on the symmetry of the tree.

Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient methods have been widely used to solve large-scale sparse systems of equations efficiently. The Flexible Generalized Minimum Residue (FGMRES) iteration is a popular variation of the Minimum Residue (GMRES) iteration with adaptable memory usage. However, the original FGMRES iteration is heavily affected by its parameter choices, leading to potential instability and reducing the method's effectiveness. This paper proposes a weighted orthogonal projection (WOP) strategy to enhance the FGMRES iteration. In the proposed method, a weighted orthogonal projector is used in the residual correction step, allowing for an approximate solution to be incorporated. Theoretical convergence properties of the new method match those of the original FGMRES iteration. The proposed approach is computationally efficient, with a practical implementation that only adds one extra vector to the memory usage of standard FGMRES. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness and flexibility in handling diverse systems of equations.

We explore recent developments in ergodic theory, particularly regarding joint ergodicity within pairs of rotations on torsion groups and their extensions. Our analysis leads to a significant contribution - establishing joint ergodicity for pairs involving a rotation with a virtually abelian boundary, which addresses a long-standing open question. This achievement enables us to solve two more complex problems: the Deligne's Pairing Conjecture has been confirmed by Potocky and by Tomanec and by the current author respectively.

Inside massive molecular clouds, we find McBride et al.'s concept of superbubbles to be a key area of study. These superbubbles are formed when a large number of massive stars' supernovae explode and expand outward. McBride et al. suggest that the dust produced from pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae, as seen in their study of AESOP+, can contribute significantly to the dust within these superbubbles. However, the dust formation process from the merger of neutron stars in supernovae events has not been considered before. Using the neutron star merger event associated with GW190425 and the enhanced dust emission from beta-decay products, we propose the possibility of neutron star mergers contributing to the dust inventory within these massive molecular clouds. Additionally, we suggest observing the surrounding environment of the recently detected neutron star merger event associated with GW200109ea with the eMerlin radio interferometer, as it is potentially located at the edge of a massive molecular cloud and may provide insight into the origin of the dust emission from this event.

To enhance the performance of 3D object detection on autonomous vehicles, combining RGB and lidar-based techniques has shown promise. Each sensor offers unique image and point cloud data, allowing for the integration of dedicated detection methods tailored to individual sources. However, autonomous vehicles often rely on expensive lidar systems, and the development of a cost-effective approach using only RGB images is crucial for broader adoption. To address this challenge, we propose a novel multi-stage 3D object detection framework, using both RGB and lidar-based techniques, for autonomous vehicles operating in both far-field and near-field scenarios. Our method involves concurrent feature extraction from RGB images and lidar point clouds, followed by the use of two stage object detection processes. The first stage, tailored to far-field detections, combines lidar-based feature extraction with two classification techniques. In contrast, the second stage, optimized for near-field detections, uses a lidar-based classification technique and two regression methods. Our framework is evaluated using the Lytro dataset and demonstrates superior performance when compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, our approach exhibits performance comparable to lidar-only methods using KITTI and NuScenes datasets, with a significant reduction in processing time. Our code and dataset are available for review.

A newly developed quantum machine learning model, based on the Gaussian process, successfully assists in preparing complex quantum states corresponding to the potential energy surface. By leveraging a training set of energy values, associated with a given function, the model generates a significant number of amplitudes for low-energy states. These amplitudes are particularly difficult to obtain using conventional quantum chemistry methods. Utilizing these generated amplitudes, within a given subspace, the model performs an expansion to recreate the surface. Notably, this expansion outperforms other models that rely solely on the training set. Additionally, the model demonstrates proficiency in replicating the energy and amplitude properties of the surface, even in areas that were not directly trained upon. This suggests the model's ability to capture underlying patterns and trends, making it a valuable tool for complex quantum state preparation.

During surgery, tracking the actual organs to their predicted models is crucial for enhancing post-surgery treatment guidance. Intraoperatively acquired sensor data can effectively facilitate this tracking by mapping the real organ positions to their projected models. However, organs can move unpredictably, causing displacement and distortion, making traditional registration methods less efficient. Additionally, unexpected movements and the use of force for adjusting organs during surgery contribute to the contamination of intraoperative data with noise. To address this issue, we developed a method to register organs that is robust to noise in intraoperative data by utilizing a Bayesian-based filtering approach. This approach, leveraging information from previous measurements and organizational dynamics, is capable of predicting future organ positions and correcting deviations caused by sudden movements or data contamination. We compared this method to conventional registration techniques using synthetic data simulation and real-world surgical data, demonstrating that our approach yields more accurate results despite noise in the data. Furthermore, we validated our method through applications in real-world surgical scenarios.
